milestones.title: Pick a problem
milestones.tagline: Find one problem worth building a company around.
milestones.outcome: A one-page problem statement that names a specific person, the situation they are in, how they cope today and what it costs them.
milestones.unlocks: Pod assignment and the community channel
steps: List ten frustrating situations you have seen or lived in the last month.
Score each one against the four tests: specific, frequent, painful, reachable.
Pick the strongest one and write the problem statement using the template.
Name where you will find ten people who have this problem.

template.title: Problem statement template
template.body:
Who has this problem:
[A specific kind of person, in a specific situation]

The situation:
[When does it happen, and how often?]

The problem:
[What goes wrong, in plain words?]

How they cope today:
[The workaround, tool or habit they use now]

What it costs them:
[Time, money or stress, with a rough number if you can]

Where I will find 10 of them:
[Specific places, groups or people]

checklist: Names a specific person or group, not a broad category like 'students' or 'everyone'
Describes a recurring situation where the problem happens
Describes how people cope with the problem today
States what the problem costs them in time, money or stress
Says where the founder will find at least 10 people who have this problem
mistakes: Describing a solution and calling it a problem, for example 'there is no app for X'.
Choosing a problem you have never seen anyone else struggle with.
Describing a group too broadly to be able to find and interview them.

fields.label: Problem statement
fields.help: The situation, the problem and why it matters. At least 200 characters.

fields.label: What does it cost them?
fields.help: Time, money or stress, with a rough number if you can.

fields.label: Where will you find 10 people with this problem?

milestones.why: Everything in the next seven weeks is built on the problem you pick now, so spend this week choosing it carefully.
lookFor: The tests for whether a startup idea is good, and how to apply them to your own list
Why starting with a problem you have seen up close is an advantage

watch.title: How to Get and Evaluate Startup Ideas
watch.focus: Use the evaluation questions on each of your ten situations.

watch.title: How to Get Startup Ideas
watch.focus: Short read. Notice his advice to look for problems you have yourself.

milestones.title: Talk to users
milestones.tagline: Learn what is true by listening to ten real people.
milestones.outcome: Notes from ten real customer conversations and the three insights that matter most.
milestones.unlocks: Partner tool credits, tier 1, once partners are confirmed
steps: Message at least 20 people from your list so that 10 agree to talk.
Run ten conversations using the script. Do not pitch.
Write a summary for each conversation within an hour of finishing it.
Put all notes in one shared document and write your three insights at the top.

template.title: Conversation notes template
template.body:
Date and who (role, not just name):

Their situation:

Last time the problem happened:

What they did about it:

What it cost them:

A quote I want to remember:

Strength of signal (1 to 5) and why:

Who else should I talk to:

checklist: States that at least 10 real conversations took place
Notes link is provided and the notes are about the person's past behavior, not opinions about the idea
Lists three insights that are supported by what several people said
Names something that surprised the founder
Does not rely on compliments or hypothetical future use as evidence
mistakes: Talking about your idea for most of the call.
Counting friends who agreed to be polite as validation.
Taking notes only as opinions, with no stories about what really happened.

fields.label: How many conversations did you have?
Who did you speak to?
fields.help: Roles and contexts, not a list of names.

fields.label: Your three strongest insights
fields.help: Things several people said without being prompted.

fields.label: Link to your notes (shared so anyone with the link can view)

milestones.why: You will learn more from ten honest conversations than from any amount of reading, and the way you ask matters as much as who you ask.
lookFor: Why you should ask about the past instead of the future
How to take notes and what counts as a real signal

watch.title: How To Talk To Users
watch.focus: Write your interview questions after watching.

watch.title: How to Talk to Users
watch.focus: A second take on the same skill, from an earlier Startup School.

milestones.title: Define the solution
milestones.tagline: Decide the smallest thing that solves the sharpest part of the problem.
milestones.outcome: A one-line pitch, the core features, and a clear list of what you will not build.
steps: Reread your week 2 notes and mark the moment that hurt the most.
Write the one-line pitch using the template and test it on two people.
List three to five core features and a separate list of what you will not build.
Write down the single belief that, if wrong, would kill the idea.

template.title: One-line pitch and scope template
template.body:
One-liner:
For [who] who [problem], [product] is a [category] that [benefit], unlike [what they use today].

Core features (3 to 5):
1.
2.
3.

Not building yet:
-
-
-

Riskiest assumption:
[If this is wrong, the idea does not work]

How I will test it:
[What I will see if it is true]

checklist: The one-line pitch names who it is for, the problem, and what is different from today's alternative
Lists between three and five core features
Lists what will deliberately not be built
Names a specific riskiest assumption that can be tested
The solution clearly follows from the problem and the conversations in week 2
mistakes: Listing fifteen features because they all seem useful.
A one-liner full of words like 'platform', 'ecosystem' or 'AI-powered' with no clear benefit.
Skipping the not-building list, which is where scope creep begins.

fields.label: What you will not build yet
Your riskiest assumption and how you will test it
Link to a sketch or mockup (optional)

milestones.why: Your first product should be the smallest thing that fixes the sharpest moment from your interviews, and this talk is about exactly that kind of scoping.
lookFor: What to cut from your first version
How to decide what the smallest useful version is

watch.title: How to Build a "Minimum Viable Product"
watch.focus: Use it to write your core features and your not-building list.

milestones.title: Build a landing page
milestones.tagline: Put your idea in front of strangers and count who raises a hand.
milestones.outcome: A live landing page that collects signups or expressions of interest.
milestones.unlocks: Partner tool credits, tier 2, once partners are confirmed
steps: Write the headline, one-line explanation, three benefits and one call to action.
Build the page and connect the signup form to a sheet you can read.
Share it with at least 30 people from the right audience.
Record your visit and signup counts and what people said.

template.title: Landing page copy template
template.body:
Headline:
[Who it is for + what they get]

Subheadline:
[How it works, in one sentence]

Three benefits:
1.
2.
3.

Call to action button:
[One action]

Trust line:
[Who is behind this and why]

checklist: A live page URL is provided that a stranger can open without logging in
The page states who it is for and what they get
The page has one clear way to sign up or show interest
Reports how many people visited and how many signed up
Describes how the page was shared and with whom
mistakes: Spending the week on design instead of getting visitors.
Offering several different calls to action on the same page.
Counting your own friends' visits and signups as demand.

fields.label: Where and how did you share it?

milestones.why: A landing page lets you test your idea with strangers in a day, and the point of this week is to launch something small rather than wait until it is ready.
lookFor: Why launching early beats launching perfectly
How to get your first visitors without a budget

watch.title: The Best Way To Launch Your Startup
watch.focus: Decide where you will share your page before you build it.

milestones.title: Ship an MVP
milestones.tagline: Build something a stranger can use, even if it is rough.
milestones.outcome: A working link that a stranger can open and use to get the core benefit.
steps: Write the single flow a user must complete to get the main benefit.
Build only that flow, using the fastest method available to you.
Test it with three people while you watch, and fix what breaks.
Record a short walkthrough and write down your success measure.

template.title: MVP plan template
template.body:
The one flow (start to finish):
1.
2.
3.

How I will build it:
[Concierge, no-code, simple code]

What I am skipping on purpose:
-

Success measure:
[What would tell me it worked]

Test results (3 people):
[Where they got stuck]

checklist: A working link is provided that a stranger can open and use
Describes the one core flow that delivers the main benefit
Explains how the MVP was built, including any manual steps
Reports testing with at least three people and what broke
Scope is limited to the core flow and matches the features chosen in week 3
mistakes: Building accounts, dashboards and settings before anyone has used the core flow.
Waiting to share until it feels finished.
Not testing it with anyone before sending it to real users.

fields.label: What does it do for the user?
How did you build it? (including anything done manually)
The core flow, step by step
Who tested it, and what broke?
Link to a short walkthrough video (optional)

milestones.why: This week you ship something rough that a stranger can use, and it is fine, even expected, for parts of it to be manual.
lookFor: How to build the core flow fast
Why doing things by hand early is a strength, not a shortcut

watch.title: Tips For Technical Startup Founders
watch.focus: Useful even if you do not code, for how to move fast on a first version.

watch.title: Do Things that Don't Scale
watch.focus: Read it before you decide what to automate and what to do by hand.

milestones.title: Get first users
milestones.tagline: Ten real people using what you built, and what they told you.
milestones.outcome: Ten real users who completed the core flow, and what you learned from them.
milestones.unlocks: Leaderboard listing and the investor brief template
steps: Write down your definition of a user before you start.
Invite people personally from your week 2 interviews, your signups and the right communities.
Watch each user try the core flow and write down what they say.
Count how many came back, and decide the one change you will make next.

template.title: User log template
template.body:
Definition of a user:
[What someone must do to count]

For each user:
Name or role:
How I found them:
Did they complete the flow:
What they said, in their words:
Did they come back:

Totals:
Users:
Came back:

The one change I will make next:

checklist: States a clear definition of a user based on completing the core flow
Reports at least 10 users who match that definition
Explains how the users were found, with real outreach rather than only friends
Includes real feedback from users, ideally in their own words
Reports how many users came back and names one concrete change planned
mistakes: Counting signups or page visits as users.
Only asking friends who will say yes to be polite.
Summarising feedback in your own words and losing the actual quotes.

fields.label: How many real users completed the core flow?
What they said (use their own words)
How many came back and used it again?
The one change you will make next
Link to your user log or screenshots (optional)

milestones.why: Ten real users who completed your flow is the single strongest piece of evidence you will have, and getting them takes personal effort.
lookFor: Where the first customers of successful startups really came from
How to recruit and talk to early users one by one

watch.title: How to Get Your First Customers
watch.focus: Write a list of ten names and a message for each before you finish.

milestones.title: Pitch deck
milestones.tagline: Tell the story of your startup in ten slides and three minutes.
milestones.outcome: An 8 to 10 slide deck and a 3-minute recorded pitch.
milestones.unlocks: Eligibility for the Demo Day ranking
steps: Draft the ten slides using the structure and your real numbers from weeks 2 to 6.
Write a 400-word script and trim it to fit three minutes.
Pitch to your pod, listen to what they remember, and revise.
Record the final three-minute pitch and share both links.

template.title: Three-minute pitch script template
template.body:
Opening (20 sec):
[The problem, in a way anyone understands]

What I built (30 sec):

Proof (70 sec):
[Conversations, users, return numbers, one strong quote]

What I learned (20 sec):

Why me and why now (20 sec):

The ask (20 sec):
[One clear, specific request]

checklist: A deck link is provided that anyone with the link can open
The deck covers problem, solution, product, traction, team and an ask, in 8 to 10 slides
A recorded pitch link is provided and is intended to run about three minutes
Traction in the deck uses real numbers from the earlier milestones
The ask is specific rather than a general request for support
mistakes: Spending the pitch on market size and almost nothing on evidence.
A vague ask like 'we are looking for support'.
Reading the slides aloud instead of telling the story.

fields.label: Deck link (shared so anyone with the link can view)
Your single strongest piece of proof

milestones.why: You now have real evidence, so this week is about telling the story clearly in ten slides and three minutes.
lookFor: What to say first, and what to leave out
How the business model slide should read for early stage founders

watch.title: How to Pitch Your Startup
watch.focus: Structure your deck and script around it.

watch.title: Startup Business Models and Pricing
watch.focus: Helps with the business model slide.

milestones.title: Final submission
milestones.tagline: Update your numbers, polish your pitch, and tell investors who you are.
milestones.outcome: Updated traction numbers, your final pitch, and a one-page investor brief.
milestones.unlocks: The Demo Day ranking and the interview round
steps: Update every traction number to today and note what changed since week 6.
Polish your deck and re-record your pitch if you can make it clearly better.
Write your one-page brief using the template.
Submit your startup name, one-liner, brief, links and ask.

template.title: One-page investor brief template
template.body:
Startup name:
One-liner:

Who it is for and the problem:

Evidence (conversations and what you learned):

Traction (numbers as of today):

What changed since week 1:

What I will do in the next 90 days:

What I want from investors and mentors:

checklist: Provides a startup name and a clear one-line description
The brief explains who it is for, the problem and the evidence
Traction numbers are updated and stated honestly
States what the founder plans to do next
Includes working links to the final deck and the final pitch, and a specific ask
mistakes: Rounding numbers up or leaving out the ones that went down.
A brief that describes the product but gives no evidence.
Submitting links that nobody outside your team can open.

fields.label: One-liner (shown publicly if you are selected)
What you want from investors and mentors

milestones.why: This is your final submission, and it helps to understand how investors think about early stage companies before you write your brief.
lookFor: How fundraising works and what investors look for early
How to be honest about numbers and still tell a strong story

watch.title: How Startup Fundraising Works
watch.focus: Use it to sharpen the ask in your brief.
